Saab 340 combines a high wing and low tailplane, a layout that separates it from T-tail regional turboprops.
Saab 340 has a short rear fuselage behind the wing, reinforcing its compact proportions.
Saab 340 appears smaller and shorter overall than the ATR-42 and especially the DHC-8-300.
Yak-42: Yak-42 has three turbofan engines, with two mounted on the rear fuselage and a third fed by a dorsal intake at the base of the fin.
Yak-42 uses a T-tail with the horizontal stabilizer mounted high on the vertical tail.
Yak-42 has low-mounted swept wings rather than a high-wing layout.
Yak-42 shows a slim narrow-body fuselage of medium length with compact trijet proportions.
Yak-42 has a pointed, relatively modern nose that is less glazed than the older Tu-134 nose.
Yak-42 is generally larger and longer-bodied than the Tu-134.
Yak-42 has a broader, more blended tail-root area around the center-engine intake than the slimmer Tu-134 rear fuselage.
Yak-42 is shorter and stubbier in overall proportions than the longer Boeing 727-200.
Yak-42 lacks the pronounced S-duct intake contour seen on the Boeing 727-200 center engine.
Yak-42 has only two main landing gear legs, unlike the multi-bogie main gear arrangement of the Boeing 727-200.
Yak-42 differs from the DC-9-30 by having a third engine in the tail instead of only two rear-mounted engines.
Yak-42 differs from the MD-80 by showing a dorsal tail-root intake for the center engine.
Yak-42 has its main landing gear mounted under the wing-root and fuselage area rather than on long rear-fuselage stalks.
Yak-42 presents a clean wing planform without prominent wingtip devices.
Yak-42 has rear-mounted side engines placed low enough to flank the aft fuselage below the T-tail.
Yak-42 has a vertical tail that rises directly above the center-engine intake, creating a thick tail base.
Yak-42 is a narrow-body jet rather than a wide-body airliner, with a single-aisle fuselage width.
Yak-42 has a more substantial wing and center fuselage mass than the lighter-looking Tu-134.
Yak-42 combines a low wing, T-tail, and trijet tail intake in a classic 1980s Soviet narrow-body layout.
Yak-42 has a rear fuselage profile that stays fuller toward the tail than the slimmer two-engine DC-9 and MD-80 family.
MD-87: MD-87 has a noticeably shorter fuselage than the standard MD-80, giving the jet a compact stretched-DC-9 appearance.
MD-87 is a narrow-body twinjet with two turbofan engines mounted on the rear fuselage, one on each side.
MD-87 has a T-tail with the horizontal stabilizer mounted high on top of the vertical fin.
MD-87 carries low-mounted swept wings with no engines hung beneath them.
MD-87 has the classic rear-engined MD-80 family layout, unlike wing-engined narrow-body airliners.
MD-87 shows a long slim fuselage but in a shortened form compared with the much longer MD-90.
MD-87 has older MD-80-style rear engine nacelles rather than the more modern Boeing 717 rear fuselage treatment.
MD-87 features a pointed nose and relatively small cockpit windshield area typical of the MD-80 family.
MD-87 has a single tall vertical tail supporting the high-mounted tailplane.
MD-87 keeps the clean wing underside of the DC-9/MD-80 family because all propulsion is at the back.
MD-87 usually appears more compact between the wings and tail than an MD-80 because of its reduced body length.
MD-87 has a longer and more MD-80-style tailcone than the earlier-looking DC-9-30.
MD-87 presents classic short-to-medium-haul twinjet proportions with a long nose-to-wing section and rear-set engines.
MD-87 has a conventional tricycle landing gear arrangement beneath the fuselage and wing roots.
MD-87 sits in the small narrow-body airliner category, visually shorter than most other MD-80 family members.
MD-87 has rear fuselage engine intakes positioned just ahead of the tail, framing the aft body on both sides.
MD-87 shows the same basic wing shape as other MD-80 family jets but attached to a distinctly shorter body.
MD-87 has a smooth cylindrical fuselage without the bulkier stance seen on larger twin-aisle airliners.
MD-87 retains the classic McDonnell Douglas rear-engined silhouette rather than the Boeing 717's updated tail-area details.
MD-87 combines a shortened fuselage with MD-80 family tail and engine shapes, separating it from both the longer MD-90 and the older DC-9-30.
MD-90: MD-90 has a long, stretched single-aisle fuselage that is noticeably longer than the MD-87 and DC-9-30.
MD-90 carries two turbofan engines mounted high on the rear fuselage, one on each side.
MD-90 has larger-diameter rear engine nacelles than the MD-80 and DC-9-30.
MD-90 shows more slender, pointed engine nacelles than the smaller, stubbier nacelles on earlier MD-80-family aircraft.
MD-90 uses a classic T-tail with the horizontal stabilizer mounted at the top of the fin.
MD-90 has low-mounted swept wings with no engines suspended underneath them.
MD-90 has a clean rear fuselage with the engines tucked tightly against the body.
MD-90 has a narrow tailcone extending behind the rear-mounted engines.
MD-90 has a pointed nose and a slim cockpit section typical of the DC-9 and MD-80 lineage.
MD-90 presents a longer overall body than the more compact Boeing 717.
MD-90 has its main landing gear mounted under the fuselage center section rather than in wing pods.
MD-90 is a narrow-body jet with a long and slender profile rather than a wide or bulky fuselage.
MD-90 keeps the rear-engine, T-tail layout that separates this family from underwing-engine airliners.
MD-90 has wing roots placed well ahead of the rear engines, leaving the back half of the fuselage visually uncluttered except for the nacelles.
MD-90 has a vertical tail that rises above the engine line and supports the high-mounted horizontal tailplane.
MD-90 combines a stretched fuselage with large rear engines, unlike the shorter DC-9-30 with smaller nacelles.
MD-90 has a more modern large-engine appearance than the earlier MD-80 while retaining the same basic family shape.
MD-90 shows passenger doors spaced along a long fuselage, reinforcing its stretched proportions compared with the MD-87.
MD-90 has no wing-mounted engine pylons, leaving the undersides of both wings clean.
MD-90 has a balanced profile of long fuselage, swept low wings, rear-mounted twin turbofans, and a high T-tail.
MD-80: MD-80 has a long, slender narrow-body fuselage that is clearly longer than a DC-9-30 or Boeing 717.
MD-80 is less short and stubby than the MD-87, with more balanced nose-to-tail proportions.
MD-80 has a slightly less extreme fuselage stretch than the MD-90, giving it a more classic mid-length appearance.
MD-80 has two turbofan engines mounted at the rear fuselage, one on each side of the tail section.
MD-80 uses slim early-style rear engine nacelles rather than the larger, rounder nacelles seen on the MD-90.
MD-80 has a T-tail with the horizontal stabilizer mounted high on the vertical fin.
MD-80 has low-mounted swept wings that sit well forward of the rear-mounted engines.
MD-80 shows clean wings with no underwing engine nacelles attached beneath them.
MD-80 has a conventional narrow-body twinjet layout with the engines concentrated at the back and the wings left unobstructed.
MD-80 has a pointed nose with a relatively small cockpit window area compared with many later twinjets.
MD-80 has the classic DC-9 family rear fuselage shape, with the tailcone blending into the engine-mounted tail section.
MD-80 has a longer cabin section ahead of the wing than the shorter-bodied MD-87.
MD-80 has a fuselage that appears more stretched relative to its wingspan than the Boeing 717.
MD-80 has main landing gear mounted in fuselage-side fairings rather than in prominent wing-root pods.
MD-80 has a modest wingspan relative to its long fuselage, reinforcing its stretched family proportions.
MD-80 has rear-mounted engines that sit tight against the aft fuselage instead of hanging below the wings like on 737-family jets.
MD-80 has a tall vertical fin supporting the high tailplane above the exhaust line of the two aft engines.
MD-80 has the elongated DC-9-family body shape without the especially bulky rear-engine appearance of the MD-90.
MD-80 has a single-aisle airliner size and shape with a long tube-like fuselage and no wide-body cross section.
MD-80 has the classic McDonnell Douglas twinjet silhouette of swept low wings, aft engines, and a high T-tail.
Metroliner: Metroliner has a very long, pencil-thin fuselage that is slimmer than the Beechcraft 1900, Saab 340, and EMB-120.
Metroliner is a small twin-turboprop with one propeller engine mounted under each wing.
Metroliner has low-mounted straight to mildly tapered wings rather than a high-wing layout.
Metroliner uses turboprop nacelles set close to the fuselage on a narrow commuter-airliner wing.
Metroliner has a conventional tail with a single vertical fin and low horizontal stabilizers.
Metroliner lacks the T-tail seen on the Dornier 328.
Metroliner has smaller and lower tail surfaces than the taller tail of the Saab 340.
Metroliner has a more pointed nose than the blunter Beechcraft 1900.
Metroliner has a narrow circular-looking fuselage cross-section that gives it a tube-like appearance.
Metroliner sits relatively low to the ground on short landing gear.
Metroliner appears more elongated and lower-slung than the stubbier EMB-120.
Metroliner has a fuselage that looks less deep from belly to roof than the Beechcraft 1900.
Metroliner has a compact regional-airliner size but with unusually stretched proportions for that size class.
Metroliner shows a single fin tail arrangement rather than any twin-fin configuration.
Metroliner has a straight center wing with only mild taper, not a strongly swept wing.
Metroliner has cockpit windows integrated into a sharply tapering forward fuselage.
Metroliner has engine nacelles that do not dominate the airframe because the fuselage is so long and slim.
Metroliner has a tailplane mounted low on the rear fuselage instead of atop the fin.
Metroliner has a distinctly slender rear fuselage that continues neatly to a small conventional tail.
Metroliner combines a pointed nose, slim tube-like body, and low wing in a more delicate shape than the Saab 340 or EMB-120.
